Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- One of two doctors charged with conspiring to furnish drugs to Anna Nicole Smith before her fatal overdose in 2007 surrendered to authorities and was jailed Monday, authorities said. Anna Nicole Smith's boyfriend Howard K. Stern was among those charged last week. Dr. Khristine Eroshevich surrendered at the Van Nuys, California, jail, said police and jail officials. Bail was set at $20,000, but Eroshevich had not posted bail as of Monday afternoon. Eroshevich was charged last week along with Howard K. Stern, Smith's longtime partner and attorney; and Dr. Sandeep Kapoor. Stern and Kapoor were arrested and released from a Los Angeles County jail Thursday night after each posted a $20,000 bond. All three are charged with eight felonies, including conspiring to furnish controlled substances, unlawfully prescribing a controlled substance and obtaining fraudulent prescriptions from June 2004 through January 2007, only weeks before Smith's death. Kapoor and Eroshevich were also charged with obtaining a prescription for opiates by "fraud, deceit or misrepresentation." And each was charged with one count of obtaining a prescription for opiates by giving a false name or address, prosecutors said. "Anna was the center of a cruel tabloid feeding frenzy," Eroshevich's attorney, Adam Braun, told CNN in a statement Monday. "In the face of this, Dr. Eroshevich did her best to help the patient while protecting what little privacy Anna had left. Any actions were done with the patient's well-being in mind and were certainly not criminal." California Attorney General Jerry Brown said the doctors and Stern devised a plan to use fake names so Smith could be prescribed "thousands of pills." The former Playboy playmate and reality TV star was drugged "almost to the point of stupefaction," Brown said. "The quantity of the drugs, the variety of the drugs, the combination at any given point, and her continuing to use that -- that, to a professional, is clear evidence of addiction," Brown said Friday. "These cocktails of methadone and antidepressants and sleeping pills and Xanax, you put all that into a cocktail, it explodes and can cause death, injury and permanent morbidity and disability." Brown said Stern was the "principal enabler" in a conspiracy with two doctors for giving the "known addict" thousands of prescription pills. Stern's attorney Krista Barth said on CNN's "Larry King Live" on Friday night that she thought Brown's comments were prejudicial. "I don't think that this was something that should have been stated in a public forum," Barth said. "I think it's contrary to the rules of professional conduct regarding trial publicity. And you have to wonder why such a statement was made." Smith, 39, was pronounced dead February 8, 2007, after being found unconscious in her hotel room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida. A coroner said she died from an accidental overdose of prescription drugs. Officials said that both prescription and over-the-counter drugs were found in Smith's system, including three antidepressant or anti-anxiety drugs. Human growth hormone and chloral hydrate, a sleep medication, were also found in toxicology tests, officials said. CNN's Marc Balinsky contributed to this report.

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Authorities said Monday that Dr. Khristine Eroshevich, one of two physicians accused of taking part in a scheme to supply Anna Nicole Smith with drugs before Smith’s fatal 2007 overdose, had turned herself in and was being held in custody.

Police and jail representatives said Eroshevich surrendered at the jail in Van Nuys, California. Her bail was fixed at $20,000, which she had not paid by Monday afternoon.

Prosecutors charged Eroshevich last week alongside Dr. Sandeep Kapoor and Howard K. Stern, Smith’s longtime partner and lawyer. Stern and Kapoor were taken into custody Thursday and released from a Los Angeles County jail that night after each posted a $20,000 bond.

The three defendants each face eight felony counts. The allegations include a conspiracy to provide controlled substances, illegally prescribing such drugs and securing prescriptions through fraud between June 2004 and January 2007, just weeks before Smith died.

Kapoor and Eroshevich also were accused of using “fraud, deceit or misrepresentation” to obtain an opiate prescription. Prosecutors said both doctors additionally face one count of acquiring an opiate prescription by supplying a false name or address.

Eroshevich’s lawyer, Adam Braun, defended her actions in a statement to CNN on Monday. He said Smith had been subjected to a vicious tabloid frenzy and that Eroshevich tried to care for her while preserving the small amount of privacy she still had. According to Braun, everything the doctor did was intended to protect Smith’s welfare and was not criminal.

California Attorney General Jerry Brown alleged that Stern and the two physicians arranged for false names to be used so Smith could receive “thousands of pills.” Brown said the former Playboy Playmate and reality television personality was medicated “almost to the point of stupefaction.”

Speaking Friday, Brown said the number and range of medications, the combinations in which they were taken and Smith’s continued use of them would amount, in a professional’s view, to unmistakable proof of addiction. He warned that mixing methadone, antidepressants, sleeping medication and Xanax could create a dangerous drug cocktail capable of causing death, injury, lasting illness or disability.

Brown characterized Stern as the “principal enabler” in an alleged plot with the two doctors to provide thousands of prescription pills to a “known addict.”

On CNN’s “Larry King Live” Friday night, Stern’s attorney, Krista Barth, called Brown’s public remarks prejudicial. She said such statements should not have been made publicly, argued that they conflicted with professional-conduct rules governing pretrial publicity and questioned why Brown had made them.

Smith was 39 when she was discovered unconscious in her room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino near Hollywood, Florida. She was declared dead on February 8, 2007.

A coroner determined that her death resulted from an accidental overdose of prescription medication. Officials reported that toxicology testing detected both prescription and nonprescription substances in her body, including three medications used to treat depression or anxiety. Tests also found human growth hormone and the sleep drug chloral hydrate.

CNN’s Marc Balinsky contributed to the report.

**LOS ANGELES —** California prosecutors have filed felony charges against Anna Nicole Smith’s longtime companion and two doctors, accusing them of conspiring to obtain and furnish powerful prescription drugs to the former Playboy model under false names in the years before her fatal overdose.

Howard K. Stern, Smith’s lawyer and boyfriend, and physicians Sandeep Kapoor and Khristine Eroshevich were named in a 23-count complaint alleging a broad prescription-drug conspiracy. The charges include unlawfully prescribing controlled substances, obtaining prescriptions by fraud or misrepresentation, using false names and prescribing drugs to an addict.

Bail was set at **$20,000 for each defendant**. Stern and Eroshevich were booked and released after posting bail, while Kapoor arranged to surrender to authorities and was also expected to be released on bond.

California Attorney General Jerry Brown said the defendants used fraudulent prescriptions to provide Smith with “thousands of pills” and other medications, including opiates and sedatives. Prosecutors allege the conduct occurred from June 2004 through January 2007, shortly before Smith’s death.

The complaint says prescriptions were issued in names other than Smith’s, including aliases and the names of people around her. Authorities contend Stern helped obtain the drugs and acted as a link between Smith and the physicians. The filing does not charge any of the defendants with directly causing Smith’s death.

Prosecutors allege the doctors crossed the line from treatment to criminal conduct by supplying Smith with excessive quantities of addictive medication despite knowing, or having reason to know, that she was dependent on prescription drugs. Investigators focused on a series of prescriptions for painkillers, anti-anxiety drugs, sedatives and other controlled substances.

Defense lawyers strongly denied wrongdoing.

Stern’s attorneys said he was not a physician and relied on licensed doctors to make medical decisions. They argued that he was trying to help Smith cope with chronic pain, emotional distress and other health problems, especially after the September 2006 death of her 20-year-old son, Daniel. The defense also disputed the suggestion that prescriptions written under other names necessarily amounted to fraud, saying celebrities sometimes use aliases to protect their privacy.

Attorneys for Kapoor and Eroshevich likewise said the doctors treated Smith for legitimate medical conditions and did not intend to violate the law. They emphasized that the criminal case should not be portrayed as a homicide prosecution and said the charges did not establish that their clients’ prescriptions caused the overdose.

Smith, 39, was found unresponsive on Feb. 8, 2007, in her room at the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel and Casino in Hollywood, Florida. She was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead.

A Florida medical examiner ruled the death an **accidental overdose** caused by the combined effects of numerous prescription medications. The sedative chloral hydrate was identified as the primary drug involved, with several other medications contributing. Smith was also suffering from a bacterial infection and a high fever, factors the medical examiner said weakened her condition.

Authorities found no illegal narcotics in her system and concluded that she had not intentionally taken her own life. The death came less than five months after Daniel Smith died in the Bahamas from a separate accidental drug overdose while visiting his mother following the birth of her daughter.

The California prosecution centers on how Smith obtained prescription drugs before her death, rather than on the immediate medical cause of the Florida overdose. If convicted on the most serious counts, the defendants could face prison, although the potential sentences would depend on which charges, if any, result in convictions.
